opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was honestly one of the more surprising moments of the project for us. Genie was trained purely on videos, mostly 2D platformer gameplay footage from the internet, and crucially, those videos didn't have any action labels. So the model had to learn its own latent action space: it figured out, without being told, what kinds of changes from one frame to the next were consistent and controllable, like a character moving left or jumping.

Once we had that working on frames from the training distribution, the natural question was how far we could push it. So we started prompting it with things it had never seen. We tried images from text-to-image models, and then people on the team started drawing little sketches, really simple stick-figure-on-a-platform kinds of things. And then we tried real-world photographs.

What was striking was that, in many cases, the model would treat the prompt image as the first frame of a game. You'd pick one of the latent actions, and the character in your sketch would actually move, and the background would do things like parallax scrolling, the way it would in a real platformer. It had picked up these general notions of what's a controllable agent, what's foreground versus background, how the world should respond, and it could transfer those to images that looked nothing like its training data.

For me, that's when it clicked that this wasn't just a video model reproducing games it had memorized. It had learned something more abstract about interactivity, and that's exciting because it suggests a path toward generating essentially unlimited, diverse environments, which matters a lot for training more general agents. It's still early, and it's not perfect, but seeing a child's-drawing-style sketch become something you could actually play was a really memorable moment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so honestly a lot of it was a surprise to us, even though in hindsight it makes a lot of sense given how we trained it. Genie was trained purely on video, on hundreds of thousands of hours of publicly available 2D platformer gameplay, with no action labels at all. The model learns a latent action space on its own, basically by figuring out what changes between consecutive frames and compressing that into a small discrete set of actions. So it never sees a controller input; it just infers that "something happened here" and learns to represent that.

Because of that, the model isn't really tied to any particular game. It's learned something more general about how a frame should respond when you take one of these latent actions. So once we had it working on the video data, the natural question was, what happens if we hand it a frame it's never seen before?

We started with images generated by a text-to-image model. We'd prompt something like a side-scrolling scene with a character in a cave, feed that single frame into Genie, and then step through the latent actions. And the character would move, the camera would scroll, the scene would stay coherent. That was the first moment where we thought, okay, this is actually a foundation world model and not just a game-specific thing.

Then we got more adventurous. Some of my colleagues sketched scenes by hand, really simple drawings of a little figure and some platforms, and Genie would take that and make it controllable. And then real photographs too, which was probably the most surprising, since the training data was all games. You'd take a photo of a hallway or a bridge, and it would treat whatever looked like the agent in the scene as the thing you control.

I think what we learned from all of that is the latent actions ended up being fairly consistent across prompts. The same latent action would reliably correspond to something like move left or jump, even in images with completely different visual styles. That consistency is what makes it feel like an environment rather than just video prediction. And it opened up this idea that anyone could create a playable world from a single image, which is a pretty different way of thinking about environment generation for agents.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about Genie is that an image becomes the starting point for an interactive world. You could give it a generated image, a sketch, or a photograph, and then use actions to control how that world unfolds. That’s a different capability from generating a video that you simply watch: your inputs influence what happens next.

But I’d distinguish that from reconstructing the actual environment in a photograph. A single image doesn’t tell you everything about how a world works. The model has to infer plausible dynamics, so what you’re exploring is its interpretation of that scene.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about Genie is that it learns what makes a world controllable by watching video. It isn’t given the actions that produced each frame, so it has to learn a set of latent actions—ways of representing how things change from one frame to the next. Those become the controls you can use when you interact with it.

Then an image serves as the starting point. That could be a generated image, a sketch, or a photograph, and Genie tries to predict how that scene would evolve in response to your actions. What’s exciting is that you don’t have to build the environment and program all of its dynamics first. The model has learned something about those dynamics from video, and it can apply that to a new visual starting point.
